work_experience.title: Memory-Augmented LLM Approach for Android Bug Reproduction from Video Reports
details: Proposed two-stage memory-augmented LLM pipeline for reproducing Android GUI bugs from screen recordings, decoupling video understanding from device automation to avoid repeated per-scene VLM inference.
Evaluated against ViBR, a published VLM-based frame-accurate scene-replay approach (GPT-4o + GroundingDINO + CLIP), across 53 successful runs on 20+ real-world Android apps.
Demonstrated 25.7x latency reduction (39.4s vs 1012.1s avg per run) while preserving task-completion fidelity, suggesting memory reuse is a viable alternative to exhaustive scene-by-scene VLM replay.

AI/ML Engineer: Designed and evaluated a two-stage memory-augmented LLM method: Stage 1 performs single-pass video-to-memory extraction (structured YAML+markdown task summary) via Gemini 2.5 Pro; Stage 2 conditions closed-loop device automation on that memory, eliminating re-analysis of raw video per step.

Ran comparative evaluation against ViBR (published baseline: GPT-4o + GroundingDINO region grounding + CLIP segmentation) across 20+ Android apps using a provider-agnostic LLM abstraction (Gemini, GPT-4o, Llama, Qwen, MiniCPM), isolating method effects from model choice.
Software Developer: Implemented the two-stage pipeline as a staged, config-driven experimental harness (--stage 1/2/all) with dry-run validation for reproducible evaluation runs.
Built device automation harness (uiautomator2/ADB) with stall detection and history-windowed decision loop to execute inferred actions during evaluation.
Designed flat, versioned run-artifact schema to keep every experimental trial reproducible and auditable.

research_context.title: Memory-Augmented LLM Approach for Android Bug Reproduction from Video Reports
research_context.problem: Reproducing Android GUI bugs from screen-recorded reports typically requires per-scene visual reasoning (segmentation, region grounding, state comparison) at every replay step, incurring high latency and repeated LLM cost. This work asks whether a single video-understanding pass, cached as structured memory, can substitute for exhaustive per-step VLM reasoning.
research_context.hypothesis: A one-time video-to-memory extraction, reused as LLM context during automation, achieves comparable task reproduction while substantially reducing latency and inference calls versus frame-accurate VLM scene-replay.
research_context.method: Two-stage pipeline: (1) video-to-memory — Gemini 2.5 Pro analyzes the full bug-report video once, producing structured memory (goal, step sequence, UI elements, completion criteria); (2) memory-to-device — an LLM decision loop consumes this memory as context at each automation step, replaying the recorded task on a live device via ADB/uiautomator2, without re-analyzing the video.
research_context.baseline: ViBR (published) — segments video into action scenes via CLIP, grounds regions via GroundingDINO, and performs per-scene GPT-4o state-consistency checks with recovery retries before replaying each action. Used strictly as a comparison baseline, not part of this work's contribution.

evaluation_setup.runs: 53 successful trials of the proposed method
evaluation_setup.metrics_tracked: wall-clock duration per run, success/failure status, LLM call count (comparative)
evaluation_setup.comparison: Proposed method vs ViBR baseline on same app set

findings: Memory reuse removes the need for per-scene segmentation, region grounding, and state-consistency retries at automation time, the primary latency driver in the baseline
Single video-analysis pass sufficient to condition multi-step automation without measurable loss of task-completion ability in evaluated apps
limitations: Memory-conditioned automation depends on Stage 1 memory quality — no explicit per-step device-state verification against the recording, unlike baseline's consistency checks
Evaluation apps are relatively simple UI flows; not yet tested on tasks requiring fine-grained frame-level state disambiguation
Baseline comparison uses published ViBR implementation as-is; not re-tuned for this app set

tech_stack.proposed_method: Two-stage pipeline (Gemini 2.5 Pro video-mode: memory extraction + memory-conditioned automation)
tech_stack.baseline: ViBR — GPT-4o + GroundingDINO + CLIP/SSIM segmentation (comparison only)
tech_stack.llm_providers_supported: Gemini, GPT-4o, Llama, Qwen, MiniCPM, Gemma

projects_and_research.title: Spotify Personal Analytics Platform
details: Engineered a 4-stage Python ETL pipeline processing 71K+ Spotify streaming events, enriching metadata via Spotify Web API with custom rate limiting and exponential-backoff retry handling.
Built a genre-enrichment pipeline by joining artist-level metadata, overcoming a Spotify API limitation to enrich 13K+ tracks for downstream analytics.
Developed a two-stage lyrics ingestion pipeline (batch + retry) processing 13.8K tracks with checkpointing, multi-source API fallback, and automatic failure-based source disabling.
Designed a PostgreSQL analytics schema with materialized views, composite/partial indexes, and 16 SQL RPC functions, enabling low-latency pre-aggregated queries over streaming history.
pipeline_flow: Extraction + dedup: tracks by URI, artists/albums by name
Metadata enrichment via Spotify Web API, genre joined from artist-level data
Lyrics enrichment: batch pass then retry pass with expanded fallback
Validation: field checks, duplicate prevention, post-load verification
Materialized views refreshed for pre-aggregated reads

ingestion.description: Raw Spotify export parsing and entity dedup (tracks by URI, artists/albums by name — source data lacks artist/album URIs)

transformation.description: 4-stage Spotify Web API metadata enrichment pipeline with genre join (artist_id->genres dict built from artist fetch, joined onto tracks since track endpoint omits genre)
Custom rate limiter (180 calls/30s rolling window) with exponential backoff and Retry-After header parsing on HTTP 429

Two-pass lyrics enrichment: batch pass (2-tier fallback Genius->Musixmatch, 500-record batches, checkpoint every 10) then retry pass (3-tier fallback adds Lyrics.ovh, 100-record batches, name-cleaning regex, auto-disable source after 10 consecutive failures)

storage.description: Single denormalized fact table (streaming_history) with 22 source fields, 7 indexes incl. composite (artist, ts DESC) and partial index excluding podcasts/audiobooks

query_layer.description: 3 materialized views (monthly_stats, top_artists, top_tracks) plus 16 SQL RPC functions incl. streak detection via ROW_NUMBER()-based gaps-and-islands window function

analytics.description: K-means session clustering: StandardScaler feature scaling, k selected by highest silhouette_score across candidate range (not hardcoded), centroids inverse-transformed to original scale

quality.description: Required-field validation (rejects records missing ts), duplicate-prevention check before reload, post-load verification (row count, date-range RPC, 1000-row sample cross-check)

monitoring.description: Liveness endpoint (thin, no DB check) and ad hoc performance profiling (real psutil RSS memory + wall-clock timing, JSON vs Supabase loader comparison)

planned_architecture.multi_user_schema: users / streaming_history(user_id FK) / user_statistics / user_similarities / recommendations — full SQL documented, no migration file exists
planned_architecture.recommendation_engine: Hybrid: 60% content (same-artist join) + 30% collaborative (Jaccard on artist overlap) + 10% diversity penalty — SQL examples only, not implemented
planned_architecture.auth_security: Row-Level Security + JWT user_id extraction — designed, no auth middleware present
planned_architecture.orchestration: pg_cron jobs proposed for stats/similarity — not configured
planned_architecture.status_note: 9 other users' raw export ZIPs collected but not ingested

limitations: JSON/CSV intermediate staging, no columnar format
In-memory JSON loader still primary path in production; Supabase loader partially stubbed
future_improvements: Airflow/Prefect orchestration for enrichment + lyrics pipelines
Incremental ETL instead of full reprocessing
Parquet + object storage for raw/staged data
Complete Supabase loader stub methods (mood, discovery, sessions, milestones)

assumptions: One streaming-history JSON record represents one play event
Artist-level genre adequately approximates track-level genre
Spotify export is a static, append-only snapshot (not live-synced)
Single-user schema is authoritative; multi-user extension not yet load-bearing

engineering_decisions.reason: Dashboard queries are aggregation-heavy over full streaming_history
engineering_decisions.tradeoff: Refresh cost and staleness window, in exchange for much lower read latency

engineering_decisions.decision: Checkpointing every 10 records in lyrics/metadata pipelines
alternatives: No checkpointing, restart from scratch on failure
engineering_decisions.reason: Long-running external API calls risk failure mid-run
engineering_decisions.tradeoff: Extra I/O per checkpoint write, avoids reprocessing hours of work

engineering_decisions.decision: Artist-genre join instead of per-track genre lookup
engineering_decisions.reason: Spotify's track endpoint doesn't expose genre; only available at artist level
engineering_decisions.tradeoff: Genre accuracy is approximate for multi-genre artists, but adds coverage cheaply

engineering_decisions.decision: Denormalized single fact table instead of star schema
engineering_decisions.reason: Source data is a flat per-play-event export with no natural dimension reuse at this scale
engineering_decisions.tradeoff: Some redundant text storage, but avoids join overhead at query time

engineering_decisions.reason: Most queries filter to music-only rows
engineering_decisions.tradeoff: Smaller, faster index for the common case; podcast/audiobook queries fall back to full scan

engineering_decisions.decision: Two-pass lyrics pipeline (batch then retry) instead of one script
alternatives: Single script with all fallback tiers inline
engineering_decisions.reason: Separates fast-path fetching from slower, more aggressive fallback/retry logic
engineering_decisions.tradeoff: Duplicated logic across two scripts, but keeps the common-case path fast and simple

engineering_decisions.decision: Rate limiter + source auto-disable in metadata fetchers
engineering_decisions.reason: Prevent hitting Spotify API rate limits and wasting calls on a consistently failing source
engineering_decisions.tradeoff: More code complexity for meaningfully better reliability at scale

projects_and_research.title: NYC Mobility Forecasting — ML-Driven Taxi/Rideshare Demand Prediction System (NYC TLC Data)

Designed two-stage (classification + regression) Poisson hurdle model predicting trip demand and surge risk, improving forecast accuracy (weighted MAPE 18.77%→16.52%) and cutting prediction error (RMSE) by 43%, (MAE) by 53% over baseline Random Forest.

Built RESTful API (Python, FastAPI) serving real-time demand predictions to a React/map-based dashboard, integrated with PostgreSQL and Redis caching, containerized with Docker, and architected for free-tier cloud deployment (Oracle Cloud).

Designed two-stage (classification + regression) Poisson hurdle model to predict trip demand and surge risk, improving prediction error (RMSE) by 43% and accuracy (weighted MAPE) from 18.77% to 16.52% over baseline Random Forest.
Diagnosed data leakage and sampling bias in demand model through root-cause analysis, achieving 0.969 R² and 0.990 AUC on final model.
Engineered time-series and weather features (lag, rolling averages, precipitation, temperature) from raw NYC taxi and weather data using pandas and PySpark for demand prediction model.

Implemented data quality validation and model versioning system (Delta Lake) ensuring reproducible machine learning pipeline for demand forecasting application.
Wrote 86 automated tests (Pytest) validating data pipeline and prediction API, maintaining zero regressions through major pipeline rebuild.
